title: “FAITH CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS”—BUT WHAT MOUNTAIN WAS JESUS ACTUALLY TALKING ABOUT?
paragraphs: “FAITH CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS”—BUT WHAT MOUNTAIN WAS JESUS ACTUALLY TALKING ABOUT?
Jesus never told you to pretend your mountain isn’t real. He told you where to look when the mountain becomes bigger than you.
There are some Bible verses we know so well that we stop hearing them.
We write it beneath photographs of sunsets.
We whisper it when the diagnosis comes back.
We repeat it when the marriage is trembling.
We post it when the bills are piling up.
We tell it to the mother praying for a child who no longer wants anything to do with God.
We say it to the man sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning, staring into the darkness because nobody knows how close he is to giving up.
But what if Jesus was saying something far deeper than the slogan we have made from His words?
What if we have spent years asking God to move our mountains without first hearing the command Jesus gave immediately before He spoke about them?
Because in Mark 11, Jesus did not begin with the mountain.
Not faith in your ability to believe hard enough.
And maybe somebody reading this desperately needs that distinction, because you have secretly blamed yourself for years.
You begged God to restore something that still fell apart.
Then somewhere inside you came the terrible accusation:
Maybe my faith just wasn't strong enough.
He was never teaching His disciples how to manipulate God.
He was teaching frightened, limited human beings where confidence belongs when they encounter something human strength cannot move.
And the setting makes His words breathtaking.
Mark places this teaching during the final days before the cross.
He has confronted corruption in the temple.
A fig tree has withered after His word of judgment.
The religious establishment is moving against Him.
The shadow of Calvary is getting longer.
And somewhere along the road between Jerusalem and Bethany, surrounded by the geography of mountains, Jesus says:
Then comes the sentence Christians have repeated for centuries.
ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ...
Amēn legō hymin... hos an eipē tō orei toutō...
“Truly I say to you... whoever says to this mountain...”

Scholars have debated precisely which mountain Jesus intended His hearers to envision. Some identify the Mount of Olives, which dominated the landscape along the Bethany-Jerusalem route. Others see a deliberate reference to the Temple Mount, especially because Mark surrounds this saying with Jesus' judgment upon fruitless worship and His confrontation at the temple.
We should be humble where Scripture does not explicitly identify the mountain.
But we should not miss what Scripture makes unmistakable.
Jesus took something enormous, immovable and humanly impossible and placed it beside the power of God.
“Be taken up and thrown into the sea.”
Not something twelve men could push if they worked together.
I was here before you arrived.
I will still be here after you leave.
Maybe now you understand why this teaching has survived inside wounded hearts for two thousand years.
Because everyone eventually meets a mountain.
Sometimes your mountain has a medical name.
Sometimes it has your last name.
Sometimes it is buried in a cemetery.
Sometimes it appears on a bank statement.
Sometimes it lives inside your memories.
Sometimes nobody else can see it.
An unbelieving child can feel like a mountain.
A broken marriage can feel like a mountain.
Years of secret sin can become a mountain.
And sometimes the most terrifying mountain is the person looking back at you from the mirror.
You went back to church before.
You said, “This is the last time,” before.
Standing at the foot of something you cannot move.
That is exactly where cheap Christianity tells you to become stronger.
Jesus tells you to trust God.
Biblical faith is not pretending the mountain is small.
Biblical faith knows God is greater.
That is why the mustard seed matters.
Matthew records another occasion when Jesus told His disciples:
“If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed...”
We often hear that and immediately begin measuring ourselves.
How much faith do I have?
But the beauty of the image is precisely its smallness.
Jesus does not glorify enormous human confidence.
He directs weak human beings toward an enormous God.
A mustard seed does not boast.
And living faith, however trembling, reaches outside itself toward the One who is faithful.
That means the prayer of a shattered believer can still be faith.
Sometimes faith has no beautiful speech left.
Sometimes faith is simply a bruised soul whispering the name of Jesus one more time.
And here is where the Gospel becomes far more beautiful than motivational Christianity.
Because Jesus did not come merely to teach you how to conquer difficult circumstances.
Our greatest mountain was never merely sickness, poverty, rejection, disappointment or adversity.
Sin separated humanity from a holy God.
We could not climb our way back.
Religion could not erase our guilt.
Good behavior could not rewrite yesterday.
Our tears could not purchase forgiveness.
Our promises could not resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
We needed something only God could do.
Not by telling sinners to climb the mountain to Him...
but by coming down to us.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
The sinless Son of God walked toward Jerusalem knowing exactly what waited there.
The One who told mountains to move did not use His power to escape Calvary.
He surrendered to the Father's will.
And there, the greatest obstacle between sinful humanity and holy God was dealt with through the blood of Christ.
Then they placed Him inside a tomb.
For one horrifying Sabbath, it looked as though the mountain had won.
And Jesus Christ walked out alive.
Not “speak whatever you want into existence.”
And suddenly “faith can move mountains” becomes infinitely more beautiful.
Because Christian faith is not confidence that God must give me whatever outcome I demand.
It is confidence that the God revealed in Jesus Christ is trustworthy even when I cannot understand what He is doing.
Sometimes God leads you over it.
Sometimes He takes you around it.
Sometimes He makes a road straight through it.
And sometimes He allows the mountain to remain while transforming the person standing before it.
Paul begged for his thorn to leave.
So unanswered prayer does not automatically mean absent faith.
A mountain remaining does not automatically mean God abandoned you.
The cross itself proves that apparent defeat can become the doorway through which God accomplishes redemption.
Maybe you are living somewhere between Friday and Sunday right now.
You forgave, but it still hurts.
You obeyed, but the door still closed.
You trusted God, but the person still died.
You came back to Jesus, but temptation did not magically disappear.
and all you can see is a stone.
Do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
The disciples once stood before a sealed tomb believing the story was finished.
God was writing the sentence they could not yet see.
And perhaps this is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a phrase.
He swore he would never abandon Jesus.
The memory of Jesus looking at him.
How do you move that mountain?
After the resurrection, Jesus did not discard Peter.
Three denials met by three invitations back into love and calling.
That is what Jesus does with surrendered ruins.
He does not call evil good.
He forgives evil and transforms sinners.
He doesn't pretend the scandal never happened.
Maybe your mountain is something you caused.
It is easier to ask God to deliver us from what someone did to us than to face what we did ourselves.
Maybe your family knows the church version of you while God knows what happens when the door closes.
Maybe you have learned how to raise your hands during worship while hiding chains beneath them.
And you are terrified that if anyone knew everything...
they would never look at you the same way again.
Every night you said you would stop.
And still the Gospel invitation remains:
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves exactly how much it matters.
Grace is not God shrugging at your sin.
Grace is the holy Son of God bleeding to save you from it.
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is finally dropping your weapons.
And perhaps that is the mountain that must move first.
I'll come to God when I'm better.
Because salvation has never depended upon sinners becoming impressive enough for Christ.
It depends upon Christ being sufficient for sinners.
Not because typing words saves you.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let believers who see it pray instead of judge.

If God has already carried you through something you once believed would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the flashlight another wounded person needs while walking through their own midnight.
And send this article to the person whose mountain immediately entered your mind while reading.
Don't merely click “like” and keep scrolling.
You may never know what God does with one faithful share.
Not because financial support purchases blessing.
Christ purchased our redemption, and grace cannot be bought.
Support Christian ministry because you freely want to participate in spreading biblical truth and glorifying God through generosity—not because anyone frightened or pressured you into giving.
And beyond products, the deeper reason to stay connected is discipleship.
Not because you need another saved post.
Because eventually another mountain may appear.
And when it does, you may need to remember:
Jesus never told you to have faith in your faith.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker who has questions.
Even invite the person who does not yet believe.
Let them see that Christianity is not the story of flawless people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy Savior coming for sinners.
Because perhaps the greatest miracle is not that faith can throw a mountain into the sea.
Perhaps the miracle you desperately need to remember tonight is that Jesus can take a heart buried beneath shame and make it alive again.
He can forgive the unforgivable sinner who truly comes to Him.
He can restore what sin shattered according to His wisdom.
He can turn persecutors into apostles.
Prodigals into sons and daughters who finally came home.
And sinners into saints—not because we became powerful enough...
but because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
And seated above every mountain, every kingdom, every power, every fear, every failure and every impossible circumstance is the risen Jesus Christ.
Remember that when the mountain whispers that your story is over:
The stone that looks like the end of your story may be standing at the entrance to a resurrection only Jesus can write.
